Read only by services/dawah.py and checked on load.
Each answer was researched independently with Claude from the Qur'an, hadith, classical tafsir and scholars.

topics.title: God
topics.blurb: Does God exist, who made Him, and why does He allow suffering?

questions.q: If everything has a creator, who created God?
questions.short: Only things that begin need a maker. Allah has no beginning, so He was never made: He is the First, and everything else began because of Him.

points.title: The question misstates God
points.text: Nobody claims everything needs a creator, only everything that begins. Allah is the One who never began.

points.title: A chain cannot go back forever
points.text: If every maker needed a maker, nothing would ever have started. So the chain must stop at One who was not made.

points.title: Allah is the First
points.text: The Qur'an names Him the First, before whom there is nothing. The Prophet taught that at the start there was nothing but Allah.

points.title: Time is created too
points.text: Asking what came before assumes God is inside time. Allah is the Creator of everything, and time is part of everything, so its Creator is not bound by it. Classical theologians argued this point.

points.title: Do not spiral into the doubt
points.text: The Prophet said Shaytan whispers 'who created Allah?'. The cure is to seek refuge in Allah, say 'I believe in Allah', and stop.

islamqa.title: Who Created Allah?

discussion.text: The objection is strongest when put like this. If you say the universe needs a cause because everything needs a cause, you cannot then excuse God from the rule. That looks like special pleading. The answer is that Islam never said everything needs a cause. It says that whatever begins to exist, or depends on something else to exist, needs a cause. The Qur'an frames the question in exactly this way: were people created from nothing, or did they create themselves? Both options are absurd, so something must exist that was not brought into being. When the Prophet recited these verses, the non-Muslim Jubayr ibn Mut'im said his heart almost flew.

Think of a line of people each borrowing money from the one before. If nobody in the line owns any money of their own, no one can lend anything, however long the line is. A chain of causes works the same way: if every link only passes on existence it received, then something must exist in its own right. Al-Ghazali makes this argument in al-Iqtisad fi al-I'tiqad: an endless chain of things that each depend on another explains nothing, so the chain must end in what depends on nothing.

A sceptic can fairly reply that the universe itself might be the thing that has no cause. The Muslim answer is that the universe is made of parts that change, and what changes has a before and an after, so it began. The One who ends the chain must be different: not made of parts, not changing, and needing nothing. That is exactly how the Qur'an describes Allah in Surah al-Ikhlas, and al-Tahawi puts it in his creed as: without beginning, without end. So the question 'who created God?' asks for a maker of someone who by definition was never made, like asking what is north of the North Pole.

Honest limits: we cannot picture something with no beginning, because our minds are used to things that start. But being unable to picture something is different from it being impossible. Scholars also differ on some details of how to phrase the argument. Ibn Taymiyyah discusses the questions of time and eternity at length in Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa'l-Naql, and the theologians did not all agree with him. None of that changes the core claim that Allah is uncreated. The Prophet also warned that Shaytan pushes people down this road until they ask who created their Lord. He did not ban thought. He gave a way out of a loop that has no end.

questions.q: What proof is there that God exists?
questions.short: Three lines of evidence point to Him: the sense of God we are born with, a universe that is ordered and cannot explain itself, and the guidance He revealed.

points.title: Born with a sense of God
points.text: People are made recognising their Creator. That is why even those who deny Him call on Him in real danger.

points.title: Nothing makes itself
points.text: Things do not come from nothing, and they did not create themselves. Both options are absurd, which leaves a Creator.

points.title: Order points to design
points.text: Sun, moon, rain and plants run on fixed, precise laws. The Qur'an asks us again and again to look at them and think.

points.title: Revelation shows a wise Lawgiver
points.text: No one has matched the Qur'an's challenge, and its laws are just and merciful. That points to Someone who knows us fully.

points.title: Purpose explains our existence
points.text: We were made to know and worship Him, and life is a test. Only this gives real meaning to right, wrong and justice.

islamqa.title: Existence of God: Any Evidence?

discussion.text: The first line of evidence is the inner sense of God. The objection is that this is only upbringing, or fear. Islam does not say it is a finished belief. It says people are born with an inclination to recognise their Maker, which parents and society can build on or bury. The Prophet said every child is born on this natural disposition. The Qur'an points to the moment of real danger, when people who deny God call on Him, then go back to denying Him once they are safe. This is a pointer, not a courtroom proof, and honestly some sincere people do not feel it strongly.

The second line is the argument from beginning and design. Something cannot come from nothing, and it cannot make itself before it exists. Ibn Rushd, in al-Kashf 'an Manahij al-Adilla, said the Qur'an's own method rests on two ideas: providence, meaning that everything fits human life, and invention, meaning that living things and the heavens came into being. The verses ask us to look at day turning into night, and at the sun and moon running on a fixed course.

A sceptic will say that science explains order without God. The reply is that science describes how the laws work, and does not say why there are laws at all, or why they are so finely regular that the universe can be studied. The Qur'an does not tell us to stop investigating. It tells us to look. An honest limit is that design points to a Designer, but does not tell us which one wants what from us. That gap is why the third line, revelation, matters.

The third line is the Qur'an itself. It challenges people to produce anything like it, and it says a book from other than Allah would be full of contradictions. A reader who does not read Arabic cannot test the first claim directly, so it is best seen as an invitation to study the book, not a shortcut. Finally, if we are here with no purpose, words like justice and wrong have nothing to stand on. The Qur'an answers that we were made to know and worship Allah, in a life set up as a test.

questions.q: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there evil and suffering?
questions.short: Allah is perfectly wise, just and merciful, and we see only a small part of the picture. This life is a test with free choice, and suffering can cleanse, teach and be repaid in full in the Hereafter.

points.title: He is wise, we see little
points.text: A surgeon's cut looks cruel to a child who does not know the reason. Allah's knowledge is complete and ours is not.

points.title: Free choice brings real evil
points.text: Allah gave us the choice between good and evil. Much suffering comes from what people choose to do to each other.

points.title: This life is a test
points.text: Hardship is part of the test, not the final result. Those who endure are rewarded.

points.title: Pain can cleanse
points.text: The Prophet taught that no tiredness, illness or worry strikes a believer without Allah wiping away some of their sins by it.

points.title: Justice is completed later
points.text: No one is wronged for good. Every victim is repaid in the Hereafter, so suffering is never the last word.

islamqa.title: Why Does Allah Allow Suffering?

discussion.text: This is the hardest question, and it is strongest in this form: a good and all-powerful God could prevent a child's cancer, so either He does not care or He cannot help. Islam does not reply by saying we should not ask. It replies in steps. First, Allah tells us that He is wise and just and forbade oppression for Himself, so the suffering people cause each other is theirs, not His. Second, He owns His creation, and He is not answerable to us in the way a creature is, which is not the same as being careless.

Second, real choice needs real evil to be possible. A world where nobody could ever harm anyone would also be a world with no courage, no forgiveness and no honesty. The Qur'an says Allah showed people the two paths, and that what befalls us is partly from what our own hands have earned. Ibn al-Qayyim, in Shifa' al-'Alil, discusses at length the wisdom behind Allah allowing evil to exist. He argues that evil is never pure: the same events carry lessons, repentance and mercy that could not exist otherwise. The Prophet's own prayer says that evil is not attributed to Allah, meaning evil is not what He wants for its own sake.

Third, this life is a test, and the test is not the end. Hardship is met with patience, and patience is rewarded beyond counting. The Prophet said the believer's affair is amazing, because everything is good for him: thankful in ease, patient in hardship. He also said that pain wipes away sins. This does not mean every sufferer deserves it. It means suffering is never wasted for a believer.

Fourth, justice is completed later. No one is wronged even by the weight of an atom, and the Prophet said rights will be returned to their owners on the Day of Resurrection, even the hornless sheep will be paid back by the horned one. The sceptic will say this only works if the afterlife is real, and that is true: the answer to suffering depends on the answer to the earlier question about proof. The honest limit is that Islam does not claim we will see the reason for every single case in this life. It asks for trust in Allah's wisdom, based on what we already know of Him.

questions.q: Isn't Allah just an old Arabian moon god?
questions.short: No. 'Allah' is simply the Arabic word for the one God. The Qur'an forbids worshipping the moon and sun, and the Arabs before Islam already knew Allah as the Creator above their idols.

points.title: The Qur'an forbids moon worship
points.text: It says plainly: do not prostrate to the sun or the moon, but to Allah who created them.

points.title: Abraham rejected the sky gods
points.text: Abraham looked at a star, the moon and the sun, and said none was his Lord, because they set.

points.title: Allah was known as Creator
points.text: Pre-Islamic Arabs already said Allah made the heavens and earth. Their fault was worshipping others beside Him.

points.title: The Arabic word for God
points.text: Arab Christians and Jews also say 'Allah' for God, including in Arabic Bibles. It is not the name of an idol.
points.note: Arabic Bible translations, e.g. the Van Dyck Bible

points.title: The moon only keeps time
points.text: Islam uses the lunar calendar to keep time, including the months of Ramadan and Hajj. No prayer, verse or law is directed to the moon.

islamqa.title: Doubts of one who is interested in Islam

discussion.text: The claim goes like this: Arabia had moon worship, the crescent is a symbol of Islam, so Allah must be a moon god. Each step is weak. The crescent on mosque domes and flags became common centuries after the Prophet, and it was not a symbol of his mosque or his community. Islam counts months by the moon simply because a lunar month is easy to see, and the Qur'an says this directly: the crescents are for measuring time. When the sun eclipsed after the death of the Prophet's son, people said it was for his death, and he corrected them: the sun and moon are signs of Allah and do not eclipse for anyone's life or death.

Second, the word Allah is simply the Arabic for 'the God'. Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews use it in their own prayers and Bibles. The Prophet's father was named Abd Allah, servant of Allah, before Islam began, so the name was already known as the name of the supreme God. The Qur'an says that if you asked the pagan Arabs who created the heavens and earth, they would say Allah. Their error was adding partners beside Him. It was not who made the world.

Third, the Arabs treated their idols as go-betweens, not as rivals to Allah. The Qur'an quotes them saying they worshipped idols only to bring them closer to Allah. Their own pilgrimage call said 'there is no partner for You, except a partner You own'. The Prophet rejected even that sentence. That is the opposite of a moon god being the centre of Islam.

Fourth, the Qur'an's own argument is against sky worship. Abraham watched a star, the moon and the sun rise and set, and concluded that what sets cannot be a Lord. A later command tells Muslims not to bow to the sun or moon but to the One who made them. An honest limit: pre-Islamic Arabia did have many gods, some connected to the moon and stars, and historians debate how much each mattered. That fact does not make Allah one of them. Sharing a name or a symbol with something does not show where a belief came from, especially when the belief's own text rejects the connection.

questions.q: How can a merciful God send people to Hell?
questions.short: Allah's mercy is vast, but mercy does not cancel justice. Hell is for those who knowingly reject the truth, and Allah wrongs no one.

points.title: His mercy covers everything
points.text: In this life His mercy reaches everyone through food, air and health. His special mercy in the Hereafter is for believers.

points.title: Greater than a mother's
points.text: The Prophet saw a mother hug her child and said Allah is more merciful to His servants than she is to her child.

points.title: Justice requires a difference
points.text: Treating those who did good and those who did great evil as equal would be unjust.

points.title: No punishment without a message
points.text: Allah does not punish until a messenger has come. Judgment follows what reached a person and what they chose.

points.title: Rejection is a choice
points.text: The people of Hell admit they were warned and turned away. They shut the door on themselves.

islamqa.title: There is no contradiction between the fact that Allah is more merciful to His slaves than a mother to her child and the fact that the disbeliever will abide in Hell for eternity

discussion.text: The objection at its strongest: a truly merciful being would forgive everyone, and infinite punishment for a short life seems out of proportion. Start with what the sources say about mercy. Allah says His mercy encompasses all things. The Prophet said Allah made mercy in a hundred parts, sent one part down to earth, and it is by that one part that a mother lifts her foot from her baby, while He keeps ninety-nine for the Day of Resurrection. So the picture is not a stingy God with a small allowance of mercy. It is the reverse.

Second, mercy does not cancel justice. Imagine a judge who freed a mass murderer and told the victims' families that this was kindness. It would be mercy to one person and cruelty to many. The Qur'an says Allah does not treat those who did good and those who did great evil as equal. Allah also said He forbade oppression for Himself. Hell is not Allah being unkind. It is Allah refusing to make right and wrong the same.

Third, the question of who is punished. The Qur'an says Allah punishes only after a messenger has come, and no soul is burdened beyond what it can bear. Scholars such as Ibn Taymiyyah in al-Jawab al-Sahih and Ibn Kathir in his commentary on this verse take from it that those whom the message truly never reached are judged by their own situation, and that this is Allah's decision, not ours. We cannot say of any particular person that they are in Hell. And believers who sin are not treated like disbelievers: the Prophet said whoever has even a barley grain of faith will finally be brought out of the Fire.

Fourth, the sceptic asks about eternity. The Qur'an describes Hell as the result of knowingly turning away: its people admit they were warned, and that they would have listened if they had used their hearing and reason. The majority of classical scholars hold that Hell is endless for those who die rejecting Allah, citing verses of abiding forever. The honest limit is that this is a revealed matter: reason alone cannot measure it, and the Qur'an asks us to trust that the Judge knows every heart better than we do.

topics.title: Jesus and Christianity
topics.blurb: What Islam says about Jesus, the Trinity and the crucifixion.

questions.q: Do Muslims believe in Jesus?
questions.short: Yes. Believing in Jesus (Isa) is part of being Muslim. We honour him as one of the greatest messengers, born miraculously to the Virgin Mary, but we do not say he is God or God's son.

points.title: A mighty messenger
points.text: Jesus was a servant and messenger of Allah, sent to the Children of Israel to call them to worship Allah alone. Denying him would take a person out of Islam.

points.title: Born miraculously to Mary
points.text: Mary is the most honoured woman in the Qur'an, and Jesus was born with no father. Allah creates as He wills, as He did with Adam.

points.title: Miracles by Allah's leave
points.text: He spoke as a baby, healed the blind and the leper and raised the dead, always "by Allah's permission". The miracles prove his mission, not divinity.

points.title: Raised up, will return
points.text: Muslims believe Allah raised him alive, and he will return before the Last Day to rule justly and uphold pure monotheism.
points.note: Ibn Kathir on 4:159 and 43:61; the hadith of the descent of the son of Mary in Bukhari and Muslim

points.title: He never claimed divinity
points.text: On the Day of Resurrection Jesus will deny ever telling people to worship him and his mother. He also gave glad tidings of a messenger to come after him, named Ahmad.

islamqa.title: Muslims' Belief About Jesus

discussion.text: The strongest objection is this: if Muslims honour Jesus so highly, why stop short of what his own followers say about him? The Qur'an answers by giving him a great deal, and then refusing only the one thing it says he never claimed. It calls him the Messiah, a word from Allah given to Mary, and a spirit from Him. In the very same verse it tells the People of the Scripture not to say "three", and says he was only a messenger.

Belief in Jesus is not optional for a Muslim. The Qur'an says the believers make no distinction between any of Allah's messengers, so a person who rejected Jesus, or slandered his mother, would be rejecting the message itself. The Prophet Muhammad taught the same unity: he said he was the closest of people to Jesus in this world and the next, and that the prophets are brothers whose mothers differ but whose religion is one. That religion is worship of Allah alone.

A sceptic will say a virgin birth and raising the dead sound like signs of divinity. The Qur'an replies with a plain comparison: in Allah's sight Jesus is like Adam, whom He made from dust with neither father nor mother. If having no father made Jesus divine, Adam would have a stronger claim. The miracles are also framed carefully. Again and again the verses add "by permission of Allah", which is what a servant says, not what a sovereign says. Allah also reminds Jesus of the favours He gave him, which only makes sense if Jesus was the one receiving them.

His return is the part most people do not expect. Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir on 4:159 and 43:61, understands the Qur'an to point to Jesus coming back before the Last Day, and the Prophet described it in a hadith: the son of Mary will descend as a just ruler, break the cross and end the tax on non-Muslims. The honest limit is that the Qur'an does not spell out the return in a single unmistakable verse. Commentators record more than one reading of "before his death" in 4:159, so the belief rests mainly on the hadith, which many scholars treat as mass-transmitted.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on 4:159 and 43:61

questions.q: Why don't Muslims accept the Trinity?
questions.short: Because Islam teaches that God is absolutely One, and the Trinity makes Jesus and the Holy Spirit divine alongside Him. The Qur'an rejects this and calls Jesus a messenger and a created human being.

points.title: The Qur'an names it to refute it
points.text: It says those who claim God is 'the third of three' have disbelieved, and tells people to stop saying 'three'.

points.title: Jesus is a servant
points.text: Jesus was a messenger whose mother was a truthful woman; both ate food. Someone who needs food is not God.

points.title: Jesus never taught it
points.text: Jesus himself will disown any claim that he told people to worship him and his mother.

points.title: Not found in Islam's sources
points.text: The Qur'an mentions the doctrine only to correct it, as something some Christians say, never as something revealed to Jesus or taught in Islam. Muslim scholars say it was shaped by later church councils, not taught by Jesus.
points.note: Ibn al-Qayyim, Hidayat al-Hayara; the 'We' of the Qur'an is a royal plural, not three persons

points.title: God is One, plainly
points.text: 'Say: He is Allah, One... He begets not, nor is He begotten.' A God who needs no partner and no son is the clearest God.

islamqa.title: Is the trinity that the Christians believe in mentioned in Islam?

discussion.text: The best form of the objection is that Christians do not worship three gods. They say one God in three persons, and that the Qur'an is attacking a caricature. That is a fair challenge, and Muslims should answer it fairly. The Qur'an does not describe the doctrine's finer points. It rejects the core claims: that the Messiah is God, that he is the son of God, and that God is "the third of three". Whatever the exact wording of the creeds, saying Jesus is God is what these verses condemn.

The reasoning then runs in steps. First, the Qur'an points to ordinary human facts: Jesus and his mother both ate food, and earlier messengers had passed away before him. A being that needs food and comes after others in time does not fit what everyone means by God. Second, the Qur'an notes that Jesus himself told the Children of Israel to worship Allah, his Lord and theirs. So the worship of Jesus cannot be what he taught. Third, a God who has a son is compared to creatures, which the Qur'an says the heavens would almost split at.

A sceptic may point out that the Qur'an uses "We" for Allah, as if it hints at plurality. Ibn al-Qayyim, in Hidayat al-Hayara fi Ajwibat al-Yahud wa al-Nasara, answers that this is the plural of majesty, as a king says "we have decided", and that the Qur'an removes any doubt at once by stating that God is One. Another point is about the Holy Spirit. Muslim commentators generally read the Spirit that supported Jesus as the angel Jibril, a created being, and not a divine person.
discussion.note: Ibn al-Qayyim, Hidayat al-Hayara fi Ajwibat al-Yahud wa al-Nasara

discussion.text: Muslim scholars also make a historical claim: the doctrine took its final shape in the church councils of the fourth century, at Nicaea and Constantinople, and was not spelled out in Jesus's own words. Christians reply that it grew out of the New Testament's own language about the Father, Son and Spirit. Both sides agree the word "Trinity" is not in the Gospels, but they differ over whether the idea is there. The honest limit for a Muslim is that this final step of the argument is a matter of history. The verses above are the core of the Islamic case.
discussion.note: Historical claim: the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381)

questions.q: Was Jesus crucified?
questions.short: No. Muslims believe Jesus was neither killed nor crucified: it was made to appear so, and Allah raised him up alive. We take this from the Qur'an, and the historical record of the event is thinner than people assume.

points.title: The Qur'an is explicit
points.text: 'They did not kill him, nor crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them.' Allah raised him up to Himself.

points.title: Why the belief arose
points.text: Someone was made to resemble Jesus, so those who saw the event could honestly think it was him. Classical tafsir differs on who that was.

points.title: Those who claim to know, only guess
points.text: The same verse says those who differ about it are in doubt and follow only conjecture, with no certain knowledge.

points.title: Eyewitness record is thin
points.text: Mark says the disciples fled and only some women watched from a distance, though John places one disciple near the cross. The Gospels are reports, not proof either way, and Muslims rest this belief on the Qur'an, not on the Gospels.
points.note: Gospel of Mark 14:50 and 15:40; Gospel of John 19:26

points.title: Allah protects His messengers
points.text: Allah promised to save Jesus from his enemies, and Allah's plan prevails.

islamqa.title: Don't the Christians have the right to believe in the crucifixion, as they saw it with their own eyes?

discussion.text: The strongest objection is historical. The crucifixion of Jesus is reported in all four Gospels, and Roman and Jewish writers such as Tacitus and Josephus mention it, so how can Muslims deny it? The Islamic answer begins by being precise. The Qur'an does not deny that people believed Jesus was crucified, and it does not deny that a crucifixion took place. It says that they did not kill him or crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them, and it says that those who differ over it are in doubt and follow only assumption.

So the reasoning is about certainty, and it is honest that the earliest outsider sources are not eyewitnesses. They report what Christians said happened. The Gospels themselves also show how thin the direct witness is. Mark says all the disciples left him and fled, and that women watched from a distance. John differs slightly and places one disciple near the cross. Muslims do not use this to prove their case, since the Qur'an is the basis of the belief. They use it only to show that the claim is less certain than it feels.
discussion.note: Gospel of Mark 14:50 and 15:40; Gospel of John 19:26; Tacitus, Annals 15.44; Josephus, Antiquities 18.3

discussion.text: Classical commentators explain how the mistake could happen. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, in their tafsirs of 4:157, report that Allah cast the likeness of Jesus on another man, so those who came to seize him took that man instead. They differ on who he was. Some reports say a volunteer among his companions, others name someone else, and none of these reports comes from the Qur'an or an authentic saying of the Prophet. That is a real limit: the Qur'an says "it was made to appear so" without naming the person.
discussion.note: al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan, and Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on 4:157

discussion.text: The theological argument is that Allah promised to take Jesus and raise him, to purify him from those who disbelieved, and to restrain the Children of Israel from him. A messenger with clear proofs whom Allah has promised to protect is not left to be killed as a criminal. One caution is that the word in 3:55, "mutawaffika", is read by some early commentators as "I will take you" in sleep or death, but the majority understand it as taking him up alive, since 4:158 says Allah raised him to Himself.

topics.title: The Prophet ﷺ
topics.blurb: Who Muhammad ﷺ was, and the accusations made against him.

questions.q: Didn't Muhammad copy the Qur'an from the Bible?
questions.short: No. He could not read or write, no Arabic Bible existed in his lifetime, and no teacher is known who could have taught him. The Qur'an also corrects the Bible on key points, so it is not a copy.

points.title: He could not read
points.text: He was unlettered, and the Qur'an told this to people who knew him all his life. Had it been false, they could easily have refuted it.

points.title: No Arabic Bible existed
points.text: No Arabic Bible translation from before his time is known; the earliest surviving Arabic versions come well after his death. There was no Arabic text for him to copy from.
points.note: Bruce Metzger on early Bible translations, cited in IslamQA 487612

points.title: No teacher can be named
points.text: Enemies said a man taught him, but the Qur'an answers that the man's tongue was foreign while the Qur'an is clear Arabic. Brief meetings with Bahira or Waraqah cannot account for a whole book.

points.title: It corrects the Bible
points.text: The Qur'an disagrees with the Bible on points such as the crucifixion and the sins of prophets. A copyist would not correct his source; the Qur'an says it confirms and judges over earlier scripture.

points.title: Knowledge of the unseen
points.text: After telling past stories, the Qur'an says he was not there and knew them only by revelation. Shared stories are what you expect if both come from the same God.

islamqa.title: The claim that the Quran was plagiarized from the scriptures of the People of the Book

discussion.text: The strongest form of the objection is this: the Qur'an tells stories of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Mary and Jesus that also appear in the Bible, so surely the author borrowed them. To copy a book you need three things: access to the source, the ability to read it, and a reason to keep the parts you agree with and change the rest. The evidence for each is weak.

First, ability. The Qur'an says he did not read any book before it, nor write one with his hand, and it says this to the very people who had lived beside him for forty years. A false claim of that kind would be easy to expose. Second, access. No Arabic translation of the Bible from before his time is known, and Bruce Metzger's survey of early versions places the earliest Arabic translations well after his death. Copying would have meant a source in Syriac, Greek or Hebrew, which no one claims he knew.
discussion.note: Bruce Metzger on early Bible translations, as cited in IslamQA 487612

discussion.text: The classical answer to the claim that a human teacher helped him is in the Qur'an itself. It names the accusation, that a man taught him, and replies that the man's tongue is foreign while this is clear Arabic. Al-Tabari, in his Tafsir on this verse, records several names suggested for the man, mostly foreign craftsmen in Makkah, and none is described as a scholar of scripture. The other accusation, that others dictated old tales to him morning and evening, is likewise recorded and answered.

Then there is the pattern of the borrowing. A copyist keeps what his source says. The Qur'an instead disagrees on central points: it denies the crucifixion, it clears the prophets of the sins the Bible attributes to some of them, and it describes itself as confirming what came before while standing as a judge over it. Ibn Taymiyya's al-Jawab al-Sahih discusses this at length. The honest limit is that similarity of stories is real, and the Qur'an does not deny it. Its explanation is a shared source, not borrowing, and it says he knew none of these events by being present.

questions.q: Why did the Prophet marry Aisha so young?
questions.short: Authentic reports say the marriage was contracted when Aisha was six and began at nine, which was normal in 7th-century Arabia. No one at the time, friend or enemy, objected, and she became one of the greatest scholars of the ummah.

points.title: The report is clear
points.text: Bukhari and Muslim report she was six at the contract and nine when she joined him. Muslims accept this and do not soften it.

points.title: Normal in that world
points.text: Marriage at puberty was common in Arabia and elsewhere at the time. The early sources record no objection to it, though his opponents attacked him over many other things.

points.title: Desire does not explain it
points.text: She was his only virgin wife, and all the others had been married before. He was faithful to one wife, Khadijah, who was older than him, for about 25 years.

points.title: She carried his teaching
points.text: Aisha lived about 47 years after him and narrated over 2,000 hadith. Senior companions came to her to settle questions of law.
points.note: al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, on Aisha

points.title: Blessed by her family
points.text: Her father Abu Bakr, his closest friend, welcomed the marriage. She later spoke of her life with him with love.

islamqa.title: The reason why the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) married 'Aa'ishah despite the age difference

discussion.text: Muslims do not deny the report. Bukhari records Aisha herself saying that the Prophet married her when she was six and that the marriage began when she was nine. The objection, at its strongest, is that a child cannot consent and that no era's customs make that right. That deserves a plain answer, not a dodge.

The first part of the answer is historical. In seventh century Arabia, and in most societies for most of history, marriage followed puberty and was arranged between families. Early biographies record that Aisha had already been promised in marriage to another man, Jubayr ibn Mut'im, before the Prophet. Nothing in the early sources shows anyone, friend or enemy, treating her marriage as shocking, although his opponents attacked him over many things. That is evidence about how people then saw it. It is not proof that the accusation was never made, because we only have what the sources kept.
discussion.note: IslamQA 44990; Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, on Aisha

discussion.text: The second part is that the marriage was not consummated at six. Scholars such as Ibn Hajar, in Fath al-Bari on this hadith, explain that she joined him only at nine, when she was physically ready, and that the wait itself shows the marriage was not rushed. Her later life tells us what the relationship was. She spoke of him with love, and she became one of the great scholars of the community. Al-Dhahabi, in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, says she was among the most learned in law, and senior companions came to her when they disagreed.
discussion.note: Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari; al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala

discussion.text: The honest limit is this. A modern reader may still feel that a marriage at that age is wrong by today's standards, and Muslims are not required to say the seventh century world was the same as ours. What the evidence supports is narrower: the marriage was lawful and ordinary in its time, it was not driven by desire as the accusation says, since every other wife had been married before and he stayed with a single older wife for about 25 years, and it produced a woman whose knowledge served the community for decades. Modern laws set their own minimum ages, and Muslims living under them follow them.

questions.q: Why did the Prophet have so many wives?
questions.short: He had one wife, Khadijah, until he was about 50, and most of his later wives were widows or divorcees. Each marriage had a purpose: care, alliances and teaching.

points.title: One wife until fifty
points.text: He married Khadijah, an older woman who had been married before, at 25 and took no other wife for about 25 years. A man led by desire does not live that way in his prime.

points.title: Mostly widows and divorcees
points.text: Apart from Aisha, all his wives had been married before, and several were widows of men killed for Islam. Marriage gave them a home and dignity.

points.title: Bonds between tribes
points.text: Reports say marriages to women of different clans, such as Juwayriyah and Umm Habibah, the daughter of Abu Sufyan, built ties with tribes that had been hostile.

points.title: Teachers of his home life
points.text: His wives taught the community what only they saw at home, including rulings for women. Aisha and Umm Salamah are the best-known examples.

points.title: A ruling for him alone
points.text: Believers are limited to four wives; the Qur'an gave the Prophet a specific exception, then forbade him from taking more.

islamqa.title: The wisdom behind the Prophet's marrying more than four wives

discussion.text: The objection, at its strongest, is that a leader who took many wives looks like a man who indulged himself, and that a religion calling him the best example should not excuse it. The way to test this is to look at the pattern of his life, not at the number alone.

The pattern is the opposite of what the objection predicts. He married Khadijah at 25 and stayed with her alone until she died, when he was about fifty, all through his youth and prime. Ibn Kathir, in al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah, describes her as the wife he never forgot. It was only after her death, and mostly in the last ten years of his life, when he was leader of a community at war, that the other marriages happened. With the exception of Aisha, every wife had been married before, and several were widows of men who died for the faith, women who otherwise had little protection in that society.

Reasons beyond companionship are recorded. The biographers report that some marriages built ties with tribes that had been hostile, such as the marriage to Umm Habibah, daughter of Abu Sufyan, who had fought him. Others created teachers: Aisha and Umm Salamah passed on what only a wife could see of his private life and rulings on women's matters, which the community relied on for generations. Muslims read these as real reasons, but the sources give them as reports of wisdom, not as statements the Prophet himself made in every case.

The legal side is often missed. The Qur'an limits believers to four wives and gave the Prophet a specific exception, then closed it: no more women were lawful for him afterwards. Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir treats this as a ruling for him alone, not a model. The honest limit is that a sceptic may still not be persuaded by wisdom arguments, since motives cannot be proven. What can be shown is that the record fits the account of duty and does not fit the account of appetite.

questions.q: Is Muhammad mentioned in earlier scriptures?
questions.short: The Qur'an says he is described in the Torah and Gospel, and Muslims point to Deuteronomy 18:18 and John 14 to 16. Jews and Christians read these passages differently, so this is a Muslim reading, not a shared one.

points.title: The Qur'an makes the claim
points.text: It says the unlettered Prophet is written of in the Torah and Gospel, and that Jesus announced a messenger named Ahmad.

points.title: A prophet like Moses
points.text: Deuteronomy 18:18 promises a prophet like Moses from the 'brothers' of Israel. Muslims read the brothers as the Ishmaelites; like Moses, Muhammad brought a law and led a nation.
points.note: IslamQA 44018; Christians usually read it as Jesus, Jews as Joshua or later prophets

points.title: The one who comes after
points.text: In John 14 to 16 Jesus promises one who will speak what he hears and guide to all truth. Muslims see Muhammad; Christians read it as the Holy Spirit.

points.title: Paran and Makkah
points.text: Deuteronomy 33:2 names Sinai, Seir and Paran, and Genesis 21:21 places Ishmael in the wilderness of Paran. Muslims read these as Moses, Jesus and Muhammad.

points.title: Earlier texts were changed
points.text: Muslims believe the Bible we have is not the original revelation, so the clearest wording may be lost. The Qur'an says some wrote the book with their own hands and attributed it to God, and it is the standard earlier scripture is judged by.

islamqa.title: Is the Prophet Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allaah be upon him) Mentioned in the Bible?

discussion.text: The claim needs care, because it is a Muslim reading of Jewish and Christian texts and those communities do not share it. The Qur'an says the unlettered Prophet is written of in their scriptures, and that the People of the Book recognise him as they recognise their own sons. It also says Jesus announced a messenger to come after him named Ahmad. That is a claim about what the texts say. It is not evidence a Jew or Christian would accept as neutral.

The two passages Muslims cite most are Deuteronomy 18:18 and the promises about a helper in John 14 to 16. In Deuteronomy God promises a prophet like Moses from among the brothers of Israel. Muslims note that Moses brought a law, fought and led a nation, as Muhammad did, and read brothers as the Ishmaelites, cousins of Israel. Christians read the verse as Jesus, and many Jews as Joshua or the line of prophets. Ibn Taymiyya in al-Jawab al-Sahih and Ibn al-Qayyim in Hidayat al-Hayara develop the Muslim reading. In John, Jesus promises one who speaks what he hears. Christians identify this with the Holy Spirit, and the Muslim reading depends on arguing the wording fits a human messenger.
discussion.note: IslamQA 44018; Ibn Taymiyya, al-Jawab al-Sahih; Ibn al-Qayyim, Hidayat al-Hayara

discussion.text: Why would the wording not be clearer? The Muslim answer is that the earlier books were not preserved in their original form, and the Qur'an says some people wrote a book with their own hands and attributed it to God. So the passages that remain are read as traces. The sceptic's reply is that this makes the argument circular: the texts are used as proof, but where they disagree, they are said to be altered. That is a fair objection.

The honest conclusion is limited. For a Muslim the Qur'an is the evidence, and the Bible passages are supporting hints. For a non-Muslim they are a fair topic of study but not a proof. The argument stands or falls on whether the Qur'an is from God, which is settled by other evidence and not by these verses.

topics.title: The Qur'an
topics.blurb: Has it changed, does it contradict itself, and why believe it is from God?

questions.q: Hasn't the Qur'an been changed over time, like other scriptures?
questions.short: No. God promised to guard the Qur'an, and history fits: it was written down in the Prophet's lifetime, gathered into one book within two years of his death, and checked against the memory of huge numbers of people.

points.title: God promised to guard it
points.text: The Qur'an says God sent down the Reminder and He Himself will protect it. The history below is what you would expect if that promise is true.

points.title: Written in the Prophet's time
points.text: Even his opponents said he had the revelation written down. Abu Bakr later reminded Zayd that he used to write it for the Prophet, and companions memorised it from him. It was never a late collection of oral stories.

points.title: Gathered by Abu Bakr
points.text: After many reciters died at Yamama, Zayd ibn Thabit collected the whole text from what was written and what people had memorised. It was a safeguard, not a rewrite.
points.note: Sahih al-Bukhari, Virtues of the Qur'an, the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit

points.title: Uthman's copies matched
points.text: When recitation began to differ in new lands, Uthman had copies made from that collection and sent them out. Today's Qur'ans trace to these, and the early manuscripts that survive agree with them in the main text, apart from small differences of spelling and marking.
points.note: Sahih al-Bukhari, Virtues of the Qur'an, the hadith of Hudhayfah

points.title: The al-Hajjaj story fails
points.text: The claim that al-Hajjaj changed eleven letters rests on a narrator, 'Abbad ibn Suhayb, whom scholars reject. What al-Hajjaj is said to have done, at the ruler's order, is add marks to help non-Arabs read. No change could pass unseen with memorisers and copies in every land.

islamqa.title: Claims that the Qur'aan has been distorted

discussion.text: The sceptic's objection is fair. Other scriptures were edited, translated and copied by hand over centuries, and the Qur'an was, at first, mostly spoken and memorised. Surely a text that lived in memory for years, was collected after a war, and was then standardised by a ruler who ordered other copies burned has had time to change? That is the strongest form of the worry, and it deserves a straight answer, not a slogan.

The answer is that the text was protected by three independent checks, not one. It was written down in the Prophet's lifetime, it was memorised by many companions, and it was recited aloud in daily prayer. When Abu Bakr had it gathered after the battle of Yamama, Zayd ibn Thabit, who had himself written revelation for the Prophet, worked from the written pieces and from what people knew by heart. The point of the gathering was to keep the text safe, not to decide what it was.

Uthman's step is often misread. Hudhayfah saw people in different lands disputing over how to recite. Uthman borrowed the pages kept with Hafsah, had them copied by a committee, and told them that where they differed they should write in the dialect of Quraysh, since the Qur'an came down in it. He then sent a copy to each major city and ordered personal pages that differed to be burned. Classical scholars such as Ibn Hajar, in Fath al-Bari, explain this as ending a dispute, not deleting content.

Now the honest limits. The claim that God guards the text is a belief; a sceptic will only accept the history, and the history is strong but not spotless. The accepted readings differ in small ways of pronunciation and vowelling, and scholars record them openly. Some manuscript researchers, for example Sadeghi and Goudarzi in their study of the Sana'a palimpsest, argue that its erased lower text shows a few variants. Muslim scholars answer that such rare, private pages do not touch the text that whole communities recited and copied every day. And the al-Hajjaj story is weak on its own terms: al-Hajjaj is said only to have added marks to help non-Arabs read correctly, at the ruler's order.
discussion.note: IslamQA 23487; Sadeghi and Goudarzi, Sana'a 1 and the Origins of the Qur'an (Der Islam, 2012)

questions.q: Why should I believe the Qur'an is from God?
questions.short: The Qur'an challenged the best Arabic speakers of its day to produce even one chapter like it, and nobody has in 1,400 years. It also foretold Rome's comeback against Persia, which happened.

points.title: An open challenge
points.text: The Qur'an dares doubters to bring the like of the whole Qur'an, then ten chapters, then one, with any help they wish. A forger would not stake everything on such a test.

points.title: Its own people could not answer
points.text: The Arabs prized eloquence and had every motive to silence him. They chose war and boycott instead, and Musaylimah's attempt became a joke.
points.note: Ibn Kathir, al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, on Musaylimah

points.title: A prophecy that came true
points.text: Surah al-Rum, revealed while Persia was crushing Rome, said Rome would win within a few years. It did.

points.title: No contradiction found
points.text: The Qur'an says a book from other than God would hold much contradiction. Revealed over 23 years in changing situations, it holds none.

points.title: A sign that lasts
points.text: Earlier prophets brought signs seen once. The final message came with a sign anyone can still examine: the book itself.

islamqa.title: Miraculous aspects of the Holy Qur'an

discussion.text: The sceptic says: beauty is a matter of taste, so a challenge to match a book's style proves nothing. Many people admire other books deeply, and one could say the Qur'an is simply the best of its kind. If that is all the challenge were, the objection would win. So it helps to see exactly what is being claimed.

The challenge has a shape. It was made in Makkah, among people who judged speech for a living. It came in steps: the whole Qur'an, then ten chapters, then a single chapter, with anyone they liked to help. It also says plainly that they would fail. A man making up a book has every reason to avoid a test like that, because one good rival text would end his claim in a day.

What did the Arabs do? They did not answer with a chapter. They fought, boycotted and mocked, which are the acts of people who cannot win by words. The known attempt, Musaylimah's, was remembered as a joke even by his own side. Later scholars tried to explain why the Qur'an is unmatched: al-Baqillani in I'jaz al-Qur'an and Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani in Dala'il al-I'jaz both argue it lies in the way meaning and wording fit together, not in rare words. Be careful with the claim that nobody has ever tried; the fair claim is that no attempt has been accepted as equal by those who know the language.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, on Musaylimah; al-Baqillani, I'jaz al-Qur'an; al-Jurjani, Dala'il al-I'jaz

discussion.text: The prophecy about Rome is a second line of evidence, since it does not depend on taste. When the verses came down, Persia had beaten Rome badly, and few would have bet on a Roman recovery. The Qur'an said Rome would win within a few years, and Rome did turn the war around. A sceptic may reply that the dates are debated and that a lucky guess is possible. Scholars do differ on exactly which Roman victory and date is meant. So the prophecy works best as one piece among several, not as a proof on its own.

The honest conclusion is that this is a cumulative case. A book with a public challenge, a record of unanswered claims, a checkable prophecy, and no internal contradiction over 23 years is harder to explain as human than any one of those points alone. It also stays open to inspection today, which is the point of the last verse: the sign is the book itself, and anyone can read it.

questions.q: Does the Qur'an contain scientific mistakes?
questions.short: No error has been shown once the Arabic is read properly. The Qur'an is a book of guidance, not a science textbook, and most alleged mistakes come from a poor translation or a forced reading.

points.title: Name the verse first
points.text: Ask which verse and which Arabic word. Many claimed errors vanish once the word's range of meaning is checked in classical dictionaries and tafsir.
points.note: Classical tafsir such as Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari

points.title: A book of guidance
points.text: It calls itself a blessed book to be reflected on and a clarification of guidance. It speaks of the sky, earth and human creation to point to God, not to teach physics.

points.title: It invites investigation
points.text: It tells people again and again to study the universe and themselves, promising the signs will become clear. It does not fear inquiry.

points.title: Facts, not passing theories
points.text: Established facts are weighed against the text, but a changing theory should not overrule it. Clear revelation and sound reason do not truly conflict.
points.note: Ibn Taymiyyah, Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa'l-Naql

points.title: Test one example
points.text: The verse says sun and moon each glide in an orbit. The Arabic verb means to float or glide, not to be fixed in place, which is a fair fit with what we now know, though it is not a lesson in astronomy.

discussion.text: The sceptic points to particular verses and asks why they should not be read at face value. A well-known one says Dhul-Qarnayn found the sun setting in a spring of murky water. Read as a claim about astronomy, that would be a mistake. So the question is whether the Qur'an is making that claim, or describing what a traveller saw.

The first step is to ask what kind of book it says it is. It calls itself a blessed book to be reflected upon, and a clarification of guidance for people who submit. Its verses on the sky, the earth and human creation are given as signs that point to God, not as lessons in physics. Judging it as a textbook is judging it by a standard it never set for itself.

The second step is language. Arabic words often have a range of meaning, and the classical commentators, such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, read many of these verses as describing appearances or events in a story, without ruling on physical fact. Take the sun and moon each moving in an orbit. The verb means to glide or float, which is different from being fixed to a sphere. That is a fair reading; it is not proof that the verse teaches modern astronomy, and nobody should claim more.

The third step is how to weigh science against scripture. Ibn Taymiyyah argued that clear revelation and sound reason cannot truly contradict, so when they seem to, either the reading of the text or the claim of reason is faulty. The sceptic will say that this can protect the text from any test. The reply is that the rule has two sides: a settled fact does push us to re-read a verse, but a passing theory should not overturn the text. The danger to avoid on the other side is forcing every new discovery into a verse after the fact.
discussion.note: Ibn Taymiyyah, Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa'l-Naql

discussion.text: Finally, the book itself does not fear the question. It tells people to look at the universe and at themselves, and promises that the signs will become clear to them. A text that asks for investigation is not behaving like one that is hiding from it. If you have a specific verse in mind, the best course is to bring it, with its Arabic, and look at it on its own terms.

topics.title: Miracles of the Qur'an
topics.blurb: Its language, its predictions and history, and why the signs add up to proof.

questions.q: What is the Qur'an's language miracle?
questions.short: The Qur'an challenged the most eloquent people in history to produce even one short surah like it, and they never did, though they had every reason to. Its form is neither poetry nor prose. No attempt since has been accepted as matching it.

points.title: An open challenge
points.text: First to bring a book like it, then ten surahs, then a single surah. The shortest surah, al-Kawthar, is only three short verses.

points.title: Answered in advance
points.text: It said outright 'you will never do it'. One successful surah would have undercut its central claim in public, so the claim was fully exposed to failure.

points.title: The best placed to answer
points.text: Poetry was the Arabs' highest art, and Quraysh were desperate to stop him. They chose war, exile and loss of life over the easy route of composing one surah.

points.title: Neither poetry nor prose
points.text: Opponents tried to call it poetry, magic or soothsaying and could not settle on a label, because it fits none of their known forms. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, a master of verse, could only call it magic.

points.title: So it is not human speech
points.text: Those most able, most motivated and given the most time all failed. If a human could make it, a human could match it. The fitting conclusion is that it comes from God.

islamqa.title: Miraculous aspects of the Holy Qur’an

discussion.text: The strongest objection is that eloquence is a matter of taste. Nobody can measure it, and a challenge judged by believers proves nothing. There is also the thought that Quraysh simply did not bother. The reply starts with who was tested. The challenge was made in public, in Makkah, to the people who lived for the spoken word and who held poetry contests at their markets. The judges were the opponents themselves. They wanted to silence him and had every reason to answer. The bar was also low: a single surah, and the shortest is only three verses.

Now the reasoning, step by step. First, the claim was public and specific: it said they could not do it. Second, failing cost them everything, since he kept winning followers, and succeeding would cost only a few lines of verse. Third, they were known to answer insults with satire, which they did in verse against him. Fourth, they turned to boycott, war and exile instead. The simplest reading is that they tried, or knew better than to try, and could not produce something people would accept. Ibn Kathir makes this argument in his tafsir of 2:23-24, and al-Baqillani builds the case at length in I'jaz al-Qur'an.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir, on 2:23-24; al-Baqillani, I'jaz al-Qur'an

discussion.text: What kind of speech is it? Reports say al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, a respected man of Quraysh, was asked to judge it. He said it was not poetry, not the talk of a soothsayer, and that it had a sweetness to it, yet in the end he settled on 'magic', so as not to have to accept it. The Qur'an records his last word. The point is not this one story, whose chain scholars discuss. It is that the Qur'an has rhyme and rhythm, but no poetic metre, and it is not ordinary prose. The Arabs had no name for it, and it is why the Qur'an says it is neither the word of a poet nor of a soothsayer.

Honest limits. First, this sign can be tested first-hand only by a person who knows Arabic well, so others must rely on those who do. Translation loses it. Second, scholars differed on where the miracle lies. Al-Jurjani (Dala'il al-I'jaz) located it in the arrangement of words, and most scholars agreed. A minority, such as the Mu'tazili al-Nazzam, said God simply turned people away from trying (the 'sarfa' view). Most scholars rejected that, because the text itself is what astonishes. Third, later claimants such as Musaylimah produced rhymed sayings that even his own followers found weak. The claim is not that imitation is logically impossible, but that after fourteen centuries no attempt has been accepted by Arabic speakers as equal.
discussion.note: Al-Jurjani, Dala'il al-I'jaz; al-Baqillani, I'jaz al-Qur'an; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, on Musaylimah

questions.q: Did the Qur'an predict the future?
questions.short: Yes. It made specific claims about events still to come, stated in public, which could have proved it false, and they came true: the Romans' comeback after a crushing defeat, the rout of Quraysh at Badr, and the Muslims entering Makkah.

points.title: A test anyone can run
points.text: A real prediction is specific, made before the event, and could fail. Vague sayings prove nothing; these were none of those.
points.note: Reasoned standard applied to each prediction below

points.title: The Romans would win back
points.text: When Persia had crushed Byzantium, the Qur'an said the Romans would win within a few years (bid', three to nine). Abu Bakr staked a wager on it, first fixing five years, then extending it on the Prophet's advice. Heraclius's counter-attack began within that span.
points.note: Persia took Jerusalem in 614; Heraclius's winning campaign opened in 622. Tirmidhi 3193 records the wager and the extension.

points.title: Quraysh would be routed
points.text: In Makkah, when Muslims were few and weak, it said the gathering would be defeated and turn their backs. At Badr the Prophet went out from his tent reciting this very verse.
points.note: Bukhari 4876: 'A'ishah says this passage was revealed in Makkah while she was a young girl. Bukhari 4877: the Prophet recites it at Badr.

points.title: Makkah would be entered
points.text: After being turned back at Hudaybiyyah, it promised they would enter the Sacred Mosque in safety. They did the next year, then took the city.

points.title: Guesswork cannot explain it
points.text: One wrong prediction would have discredited him before friend and enemy. The ones cited here all came true, which a guesser cannot count on and only the Knower of the unseen can.

islamqa.title: Things foretold in the Quran which have come to pass

discussion.text: The sharpest objection is that prophecy stories are written after the event. If the verses about Rome were composed or adjusted after 622, the whole sign vanishes. A second objection is that the events were guessable. The reply is that a prediction only counts if it is public, specific and dated before the outcome, so each case must pass that test. The Romans case does: the verses are Makkan, the wager was made in public with the idolaters, and the event was checked by everyone who heard about it.

Consider the Roman prediction more closely. In 614 Persia took Jerusalem, and the Roman state looked close to collapse. Gibbon, no friend of Islam, wrote in Decline and Fall (chapter 46) that no prophecy could have seemed more remote from fulfilment at that moment. The verse says the Romans will overcome within 'bid'', which classical scholars gloss as three to nine years. Tirmidhi 3193 shows how honestly the report is kept: Abu Bakr first set five years, lost that term, and was told to extend it. That is not a detail a legend-maker would invent. The tradition also records a second reading of the verse (ghalabat and ghulibat), and Ibn Kathir discusses it in his tafsir of 30:2, while the standard reading is the one used here.
discussion.note: Gibbon, Decline and Fall, ch. 46; Ibn Kathir, Tafsir, on 30:2-4

discussion.text: The Badr case is about weakness. 54:45 is Makkan: A'ishah says in Bukhari that it was revealed when she was a young girl in Makkah, which is when the believers were few and beaten. At Badr, Bukhari 4877 has the Prophet going out of his tent reciting it, with Quraysh in retreat. The Makkah case is softer, because 48:27 was linked to a vision and carries 'if God wills'. Even so, it was said after the setback of Hudaybiyyah, when many companions thought the truce was a humiliation, and it promised a 'conquest near at hand', which scholars such as Ibn Kathir read as Khaybar, then the pilgrimage the next year and the taking of Makkah the year after.

Limits. The sceptic can say that a small number of hits proves little, and that we know the details from Muslim sources. Both are fair. The answer is that the Roman recovery is dated by Byzantine history, not only by Muslim reports, and that the Qur'an itself says these are signs of a Knower of the unseen, not of chance. The argument is cumulative and rests on the standard set in the first point: specific, public, prior, and open to failure.

questions.q: Does the Qur'an know things about history it could not have known?
questions.short: It tells stories of past nations that he, an unlettered man in Makkah, had no way to learn, and says so openly. Its details also fit history where the Bible's differ, such as calling Joseph's ruler a king and Moses's ruler Pharaoh.

points.title: It says he was not there
points.text: After the stories of Mary, Noah and Joseph, it states that he and his people did not know them before. His enemies alleged a human teacher, but never produced one who could account for it.

points.title: King, not Pharaoh, for Joseph
points.text: The Qur'an calls Joseph's ruler 'the king' but Moses's ruler 'Pharaoh'. Egyptians began calling their ruler Pharaoh only in the later era, while the Bible uses Pharaoh for both.
points.note: A fit with Egyptian history, not a proof on its own: Joseph's date is uncertain

points.title: It corrects, not copies
points.text: Where it tells the same stories as earlier books, it differs in key details and clears prophets of faults the Bible gives them. A copier repeats his source.

points.title: No source was in reach
points.text: No Arabic Bible existed then, and he could not read. The knowledge had no human route to him.

points.title: So it came from God
points.text: Knowledge he could not have gained, delivered openly before those who knew his whole life, points to revelation.

discussion.text: The best objection is that he did not need a book. Makkah was a trading town, he travelled to Syria, he met Christians and Jews, and stories travel by mouth. The Qur'an itself records the charge: some said another people helped him, and that these were old legends dictated to him morning and evening. This has to be answered, not waved away. The Qur'an gives its answer inside the same book: the man they pointed to spoke a foreign tongue, while the Qur'an is in clear Arabic.

Ask what the theory needs. The teacher must have existed, known the detailed material, been willing to keep quiet, and taught a man who remained in Makkah among enemies looking for exactly this evidence. Nobody produced him. The reports of contact, such as the monk Bahira or Waraqa ibn Nawfal, are brief, come with chains scholars have questioned, and describe no teaching. Meanwhile, the Qur'an says three times that these accounts were news of the unseen that neither he nor his people had known. A false claim of that kind would be easy to expose in a small town.
discussion.note: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah, on Bahira and Waraqa

discussion.text: The king and Pharaoh detail is a fit, not a proof. Genesis calls Joseph's ruler Pharaoh, but Egyptologists say the word began as 'great house', meaning the palace, and only became a title for the king himself in the New Kingdom, after the age usually assigned to Joseph. The Qur'an says 'the king' for Joseph and 'Pharaoh' for Moses, and keeps that difference. A sceptic may answer that this is chance, and that Joseph's date is itself uncertain. Both points stand. Read alongside the fact that the Qur'an corrects earlier books rather than copying them (for example, Aaron warns against the calf and the blame falls on al-Samiri, and Solomon is cleared of disbelief), the pattern suggests an independent source.
discussion.note: Egyptological usage of 'pr-aa' as a royal title from the New Kingdom; date of Joseph is debated

discussion.text: Limits. Lack of a known source is evidence, not proof, since someone can always say a source was lost. Some sceptics also raise alleged historical errors, and Muslim scholars have written replies to those; a fair reader should weigh them separately. The Qur'an itself also says that it confirms and guards what came before, so overlap is expected. The claim of this argument is narrow: the man had no reachable source, the details fit history where a copier's would not, and this adds to the other signs. Ibn Kathir also warns readers to be careful with unverified stories from earlier peoples.
discussion.note: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir, introduction, on Israelite reports

questions.q: Why does the man who brought it matter?
questions.short: The Qur'an came through a man who had never produced poetry or speeches, could not read or write, and was known for honesty. It even reproaches him, and he gained no wealth from it. So he was not a liar, and a deluded man could not have produced it. What remains is that he was truthful and it came from God.

points.title: Forty years of silence
points.text: He lived among his people for forty years before the Qur'an and produced no poetry or oratory. The Qur'an tells them to remember this: they knew his life.
points.note: His everyday speech, recorded in the hadith, reads nothing like the Qur'an.

points.title: He could not read or write
points.text: The Qur'an says he never read a book or wrote one before it, and calls him the unlettered Prophet. That rules out studying earlier writings and writing from them.

points.title: Known as the truthful one
points.text: His people called him al-Amin, the trustworthy. When Heraclius asked Abu Sufyan, then his enemy, whether they had ever accused him of lying before his claim, the answer was no.
points.note: The title al-Amin is from Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah, on the rebuilding of the Ka'bah. Bukhari 7 has Abu Sufyan's 'no'.

points.title: Reproached in his own book
points.text: The Qur'an corrects him in public: for turning from the blind man, for excusing people from battle, over the prisoners of Badr. A forger seeking authority would not write his own faults in. Nor did he gain: he died with his armour pledged for barley.

points.title: Liar, deluded, or truthful
points.text: A liar needs a motive, yet he had no gain, a clean record and a book that shames him. A deluded man could not produce a book that stays consistent and unmatched. Both fail, so the truthful messenger remains.

islamqa.title: Evidence for the truth of the Prophethood of Muhammad

discussion.text: The standard objection is that good character does not prove revelation. Many sincere founders have been honest people who truly believed what they said, and the biography comes from his followers. So the question splits into three: was he lying, was he deluded, and did he write it. The reply takes them in turn, using evidence from the other side where possible. In Bukhari 7, Abu Sufyan, still an enemy, answers Heraclius that they never accused him of lying before his claim, and says he would have lied if he had not feared being called a liar by his own companions. Heraclius drew the conclusion: a man who would not lie about people would not lie about God.
discussion.note: Al-Qadi 'Iyad, al-Shifa', on his character before prophethood

discussion.text: Then the motive. Liars usually gain wealth, power or praise. The Qur'an records him being corrected: for turning away from the blind man, for granting leave to stay behind, over the prisoners of Badr, and over what he hid in himself about Zayd's marriage. A forger writing his own book does not place his mistakes in it. As for wealth, Bukhari 2916 says he died with his armour pledged to a Jew for thirty measures of barley. The Qur'an even says his opponents did not really call him a liar, but rejected the signs. That is the Qur'an's own testimony and is reported, not proven from outside.

Delusion is harder to dismiss with character alone, so the argument uses the book. A deluded person can be sincere, but cannot produce a work that stays consistent for 23 years, includes law, history, argument and prayer, and stays unmatched. His own recorded speech in the hadith is plainly different in style from the Qur'an, and he kept the two apart. Ibn Taymiyya, in al-Jawab al-Sahih, compares true prophets with liars and the possessed, and argues that the difference shows in their message, their conduct, and what follows from them.
discussion.note: Ibn Taymiyya, al-Jawab al-Sahih li-man baddala din al-Masih

discussion.text: On being unlettered, the Qur'an calls him ummi, and 29:48 says he never read or wrote a book before. Most classical scholars, including Ibn Kathir, took this as unable to read and write. Some modern writers say ummi means 'of the gentiles', which would weaken the point, but 29:48 stands on its own words. Honest limit: this argument removes the 'liar' and 'deluded' explanations. It does not by itself prove the Qur'an is revelation. That step comes from putting it together with the other signs.

questions.q: How could a book revealed over 23 years stay consistent?
questions.short: The Qur'an came in pieces over 23 years, through war and peace, grief and victory. Yet it keeps one voice with no contradiction, as it says it would if it were from God. A human author changes over that long and revises his work; there were no drafts here.

points.title: It sets its own test
points.text: It says that if it were from anyone but God, people would find much contradiction in it. Anyone can check that claim.

points.title: Revealed in pieces, to events
points.text: It came in stages, answering events as they happened, not written in one calm sitting.

points.title: No drafts, no revisions
points.text: Each passage was recited as it came, memorised by the companions and written down by scribes. The Prophet was promised he would not forget it. Where a ruling was replaced by a later one, the Qur'an says so openly.

points.title: His own grief stays out
points.text: He wept when his son Ibrahim died, yet no verse mourns him, and when people linked an eclipse to the death he denied it. The deaths of Khadijah and Abu Talib are not lamented either; instead it told him he cannot guide whom he loves.
points.note: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah, on the deaths of Abu Talib and Khadijah

points.title: Why a human could not do it
points.text: Over 23 years a person's mood, views and style shift, and writing shaped by war and grief shows it. Here the voice holds steady and the author's feelings stay out. That points to a source beyond him.

discussion.text: The objection is twofold. First, sceptics list verses they say contradict each other, and the tone of the Makkan and Madinan surahs differs. Second, a careful author could keep a steady line, so consistency proves little. The Qur'an's test is narrow and worded carefully: 'much contradiction', not 'no change of tone'. A book that addresses a persecuted minority and later a ruling community should sound different in its style and topics. The claim is that its teaching on God, judgement, prophets and worship does not change from the first surah to the last.

Apparent conflicts have been treated in works by Muslim scholars for centuries, such as Ibn Qutayba's Ta'wil Mushkil al-Qur'an and al-Shanqiti's Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab. Most turn out to be about different questions, or general and specific statements. Abrogation is a separate case. The Qur'an says openly that God may replace a ruling with another, and the change of rulings on drinking, for example, was done in stages. That is not a slip that got corrected quietly, because it is announced in the text.
discussion.note: Ibn Qutayba, Ta'wil Mushkil al-Qur'an; al-Shanqiti, Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab

discussion.text: Then the circumstances. It came in stages, answering questions, wars, and defeats, and the Qur'an says why: to strengthen his heart. A human writing in those years would show it, and few authors keep their own feelings out of writing for 23 years. Here the speaker is always God addressing him, sometimes consoling him, never voicing his mood. Ibrahim died and he wept, and the Qur'an gave no elegy. An eclipse happened that day, and he refused the crowd's claim that it marked the death, when accepting it would have helped him. Bukhari 1303 and 1043 report both.

Honest limits. Consistency alone is the weakest of the signs, since a skilled author can be consistent. Its force is in combination: consistent over 23 years, produced in changing conditions, without drafts, and still unmatched in language. Silence about his grief is also a negative proof, so it supports the case but cannot carry it. Ibn Kathir, commenting on 4:82, treats the verse as an invitation to reflect and check, and the reader is free to do exactly that.

questions.q: Why do these signs add up to proof?
questions.short: Any one sign could be argued with alone. But they are different in kind and all true together: an unanswered challenge, fulfilled predictions, an unlettered messenger, unbroken consistency, a preserved text and a transformed people. Every other explanation fails on at least one, and only one covers them all: it is from God.

points.title: Signs of different kinds
points.text: The challenge to match it stands unmet. It foretold the Romans' comeback within a few years. It promised its own preservation. It united a people who had been enemies.

points.title: He did not write it himself
points.text: He was unlettered and had produced no such speech in forty years. He was known as honest, and the text reproaches him. Writing it himself leaves no motive and no means.

points.title: No teacher, no copying
points.text: Enemies said a man taught him; the Qur'an answers that the man speaks a foreign tongue while this is clear Arabic. Copying scripture needs reading or a teacher, and both are ruled out.

points.title: One cause fits every sign
points.text: Each other explanation breaks on at least one fact. A human author fails on 23 years of consistency, the unmet challenge and the fulfilled predictions together. Only a source beyond the man accounts for all at once.

points.title: Reflect, then conclude
points.text: The Qur'an does not ask for blind acceptance. It asks people to reflect and promises signs until the truth is clear. Once the alternatives fail, the conclusion is that it is from God.

discussion.text: The fair objection to a cumulative case is that many weak arguments do not add up to a strong one. Zero plus zero is zero. The reply accepts this: the case works only if each sign has real force by itself, and the signs must be different in kind so that one fault cannot sink them all. They are. The challenge is about the text, the Roman prediction is about dated events, the messenger is about a life, the consistency is about how the book was produced, and the union of enemies is about what followed. A rival theory has to explain each of these separately.

Take the rival explanations one at a time. He wrote it: he lacked the means and the motive, and the book reproaches him. He was taught: the accused teacher spoke a foreign tongue, and nobody produced a real source. He was deluded: a delusion does not stay consistent over 23 years or answer a public challenge. It was a group effort: then the group would have answered the challenge in Makkah. It grew as a legend: the text was recited, memorised and written down in his lifetime, and God promises to guard it. Each theory loses on at least one fact, which is why the argument stresses fit with all of them at once.

Why 'from God', and not just 'unexplained'? Because this is reasoning to the best explanation, the way we reason about any past event. When every human explanation fails and the book itself claims a source and gives a test, the source it names becomes the most reasonable remaining answer. Al-Baqillani argued in I'jaz al-Qur'an that the proof is the combination of the inimitable text and the claim it makes. A closed mind can always say 'we do not know yet', and that remains possible. But the Qur'an asks people to weigh the evidence for themselves, so the conclusion is offered, not forced.

Limits, said plainly. No historical claim can be proven the way a chemistry experiment can. The standard here is the one we accept for any past event: what a fair person can reasonably conclude from the evidence. The Qur'an itself notes that some who see the signs still reject them, and asks whether their hearts are locked. It also records people demanding other signs. So the signs give a strong reason to believe, and the last step of honest reflection is left to the reader.

topics.title: Violence and Jihad
topics.blurb: Was Islam spread by the sword, and what does jihad mean?

questions.q: Wasn't Islam spread by the sword?
questions.short: No. Armies did expand Muslim rule, but the Qur'an forbids forcing belief, and most people came to Islam over generations through trade, teaching and example. Most Muslims today live where no Muslim army ever went.

points.title: Belief cannot be forced
points.text: There is no compulsion in religion; the Prophet's job was to convey, not to control hearts.

points.title: Conquest is not conversion
points.text: Jews and Christians kept their faith under Muslim rule for centuries, paying a tax in place of military service. That is impossible if conversion was forced.
points.note: Christian and Jewish communities of Egypt, Syria and Iraq to this day

points.title: Fighting had set reasons
points.text: Fighting was permitted against those who attacked or expelled Muslims or blocked the message by force, never for disagreeing.

points.title: Many were never conquered
points.text: Indonesia, Malaysia and large parts of East and West Africa came to Islam largely through merchants and teachers, not through an invading army.
points.note: Richard Bulliet, Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period

points.title: Invitation first, always
points.text: Commanders had to invite people and offer terms before fighting, and spare women and children. Scholars who say the sword removed obstacles still held that no one is made to believe.

islamqa.title: Was Islam spread by the sword?
